sentences: At her family's rural manor in the country, the daughter celebrates her twenty-first birthday with her father the host, her suitor the challenger, and the challenger's two rivals, the first rival and the second rival.

The challenger challenges the first rival and the second rival to each spend a night in a mysterious locked blue room in which several murders had occurred years before, each at exactly one hour past midnight.
The first victim was the host's sister, followed by his best friend and, later, a detective who attempted to solve their deaths.
The challenger sleeps there on the first night but disappears exactly at 1:00 a.m.
The daughter explores the blue room alone the following day, but is attacked by an unseen assailant and loses consciousness, regaining it with no memory of her attacker's identity.
The second rival agrees to spend the night in the blue room after the host retires for the evening.
The second rival begins playing a piano in the room shortly after midnight to signal to the others that he is still alive.
Unable to sleep, the daughter is comforted by the first rival before a gunshot rings out, and the piano playing ceases.
The first rival rushes to the blue room, where he finds the second rival shot to death.
The first rival reports the second rival's murder to the commissioner.
Moments later, an alert buzzer sounds from the blue room.
The first rival enters the room to find a cat has triggered the buzzer, but cannot explain how the animal accessed the room.

The next morning, the Commissioner and his assistant the aide question the family and their guests, along with the first maid and the second maid, servants of the manor, and the manservant, the butler.
The second maid tells the Commissioner that she saw a strange man exit the blue room after the second rival's murder.
The next day, an apparent vagrant enters the manor, and the host confesses to the Commissioner in confidence that the man is his brother, who is in fact the daughter's biological father.
On the fifth night, the Commissioner oversees the manor while the first rival stays in the blue room, hoping they can apprehend the killer.
The first rival places a dummy in an armchair in the blue room and hides behind a coat.
At exactly 1:00 a.m., the assailant breaches the door to the blue room and aims a revolver at the dummy before firing.
The cloaked assailant flees into an underground corridor system that runs beneath the manor, with the first rival and the Commissioner's officers in pursuit.
Following a gunfight, the killer is apprehended and revealed to be the challenger.
The challenger confesses to killing the second rival and plotting the first rival's death out of jealousy, believing both men were threats against his relationship to the daughter.
A man comes out of the office of "the investment firm".
He meets the janitor in the stairs and asks him for a match, and then what time it is.
"It's nine" the Italian-American janitor the caretaker answers and wants to know from which apartment he came out.
The man leaves without answering.
Shortly after, the janitor finds a dead man in the office of "the investment firm".
Newspaperman the first reporter from the newspaper is there to talk with the inspector.
Before he can see him he talks with the watching police officer, and after a while, realizes that the investment firm just that morning went bankrupt.
"Another broker went down the flush".
The janitor recognizes on the police records the man who came out of the office, the suspect.
During the trial he sticks to what he has seen and what he has heard, though two different doctors testify that the suspect is deaf and mute since birth.

Young newspaper newspaperman the young reporter, in love with his good-looking girl colleague, has a feeling that the suspect is a strange guy and tries to convince her not to go for interview to his house.
Meantime a young broker tells him he has a hint, if he gets enough money for it.
The suspect comes to see the young broker before at half past eight the first reporter comes to his house.
A second time the suspect asks for the time after seeing his victim.
The puzzling case has the parallel love story of the two newspaper-people of the newspaper.
While the first reporter, who wants to marry the young reporter, is skeptical about the suspect, the young reporter is fascinated by the suspect and writes a series of articles about him.
When the inspector thinks he saw the suspect hearing the playing of the piano when they are in his house, the next morning a third dead man is on the list.

Severely agitated by the howling of a German Shepherd police dog next door, millionaire the neighbor comes to the city lawyer the attorney to draw up his will, stating that the howling is a sign that a death has occurred.

He wants to leave his money to the apparent wife of the dog owner, another millionaire and the dog's owner, explaining that while "the companion" pretends to be the dog owner's wife, he is still legally married to someone else.
The attorney explains how the neighbor should word his odd bequest and after receiving a huge retainer fee, gives him a form to fill out and return.
When the attorney receives the form the next day, the neighbor has changed the beneficiary to the dog owner's actual wife.
The fee paid by the neighbor obligates the attorney to legally and morally represent the real lawful wife to the best of his ability.
The dog owner attempts to file a complaint of insanity against the neighbor, claiming he is a homicidal maniac whose bizarre behavior prompted most of the dog owner's household staff to quit.
A sheriff's deputy is assigned to investigate the complaint.
He and the attorney accompany the dog owner back to his house, where the attorney questions why an addition to his garage is being built for yet another car if his chauffeur has quit.

Attractive the housekeeper, who the dog owner states is his housekeeper, rushes from the house with her right hand heavily bandaged to tell the dog owner that she was bitten by the dog while giving it an emetic, thinking it had been poisoned.
When they ask to talk to the dog owner's "wife" the companion, the housekeeper tells them that she has just packed her bags and disappeared.
A note left behind states that she loves the neighbor and is going away with him.
The attorney goes next door and finds that the neighbor has also disappeared overnight.
A telegram sent from a nearby town and signed by the companion is sent to the dog owner asking him to stop his actions.

The attorney's private detectives investigate and learn that the companion was actually the neighbor's wife who ran away with the dog owner when they were friends in another town with the dog owner and his wife the lawful wife.
The housekeeper was the dog owner's private secretary then, unbeknownst to the companion.
One of the attorney's men is assigned to watch the dog owner's house and sees the housekeeper drive away with an unknown man.
A cab arrives with a woman in black.
When the dog owner shows annoyance that she "found him", she tells him that she "wants justice" and he releases the dog to attack her.
Two shots are fired, killing the dog and the dog owner, followed by the slamming of the garden door, and the woman flees.
The attorney arrives for a meeting with the dog owner and discovers the bodies.

He immediately tracks down the cab driver at his cab stand, learning that a perfumed handkerchief left in the cab links "the lawful wife" to the murder scene, and then finds the woman, who is the actual wife and his client, in a hotel under an assumed name.
He sends his secretary, the assistant, to impersonate the lawful wife and claim the handkerchief before the cabbie turns it in.
The lawful wife denies killing her husband.
The attorney warns her that she is going to be arrested for the dog owner's murder and orders her to say nothing to the police.

Later, acting on a hunch when none of the handwriting samples of the three women gathered by his operatives matches the note and the handwritten copy of the telegram, the attorney devises a ruse to obtain a page from the housekeeper's diary of the day after the neighbor and his wife disappeared.
During the trial, the attorney discredits the cab driver's identification of his passenger when he demonstrates that he misidentified the assistant as the lawful wife.

During his cross-examination of the housekeeper, the attorney has the trial shifted to the scene of the crime, shows that the dog was devoted to all three women, and proves that the housekeeper was the dog owner's lover and is ambidextrous, writing the note, the telegram, and the diary page with her left hand.
Just then, workers excavating the foundation of the garage addition discover the bodies of the neighbor and the companion, murdered by the dog owner.

The lawful wife is acquitted after the attorney in closing arguments states that because the dog loved her, he would never have attacked the lawful wife and been killed, destroying the prosecution's only other link of the lawful wife to the crime.
After the trial, the attorney presents the lawful wife with a dog that looks just like the dead animal, and the dog delightedly greets the lawful wife.
The attorney states that when the howling suddenly stopped, he searched kennels in the area and found one where a man matching the dog owner's description exchanged the dog for a lookalike.
He gives the lawful wife the dog and orders her not to tell anyone what really happened.
The attorney later tells the assistant that he is sure that whatever the lawful wife did was in self-defense, and that she cannot be tried again for the murder due to double jeopardy.

The host is having dinner with his wife, the hostess, and four of their friends: the colleague, his business partner; the employee, who works at their company; and the host's sister, the married sister, and her husband, the brother-in-law, who is another partner in the firm.
As the dinner winds down, the subject of the host's brother's suicide comes up.

The host's brother, the dead brother, had died from a gunshot wound, which an investigation had ruled a suicide, brought on by his guilt over stealing a bond from their company, of which he was also a partner.
But now, during their dinner conversation, certain comments made by his companions don't add up in the host's mind.
As he begins to question them, the hostess confesses that she had been secretly in love with the dead brother, and the employee reveals that she has been carrying a torch for the host for years.

It was this unspoken love which caused the employee to not speak honestly at the hearing into the dead brother's death, for she thought that it might have been the host, not the dead brother, who stole the bond.

The married sister announces that she has been in love with the colleague, who confesses to having stolen the bond, in order to satisfy a debt owed by the married sister, even though he has been in love with the employee.
The employee then confesses that the dead brother did not commit suicide as everyone thought, but that she accidentally shot him.
Unable to deal with the guilt of all the confessions, the host leaves the room and shoots himself.

After a moment, time returns to the moment that the conversation started after dinner, but this time the brother-in-law is able to repair the radio and plays music which stops the conversation from starting.
The colleague asks the employee for hand in marriage, as he has for years, but this time she accepts.
The airline's pilot "the ace" the aviator is in love with stewardess the flight attendant, but she wants him to stop his daredevil ways.
So does his boss, the manager.
Confident in his abilities and knowing that he is the airline's best pilot, he pays neither any mind.

Federal agent the government man urgently requests the manager's cooperation: the inventor must be flown from the western city to the capital, with a cylinder full of a revolutionary new explosive he has invented.
However, the manager's assistant the clerk is eavesdropping on him for the spymaster, a spy.
He eavesdrops again when the manager chooses the aviator as pilot and the flight attendant's brother the young flyer as co-pilot.
The spymaster sends three men to provoke the aviator into a fistfight.

While the aviator is knocked out, another pilot, the substitute pilot, chats casually with the young flyer, "learns" that the aviator is late for the special trip, and offers to protect the aviator's job by taking over.
Over the lower mountains, the three-engine airliner explodes.
The aviator and the manager fly to the crash site and talk to the government man.
The young flyer's cap is there.
Back in the western city, they report that there are no survivors.
Frantic for news of her brother, the flight attendant drives to the site before they return, evading the police roadblock.
She is recognized by the clerk, who is traveling with the spies to a nearby house they are using.
Improvising a plan, they pose as federal agents and stop her.

At the house she is surprised to see the substitute pilot, who tells her the saboteur ordered him and the young flyer to parachute out, then set a bomb and himself parachuted out with the cylinder—all nearly true, except that the substitute pilot was the saboteur and the young flyer is dead.

They want to hide the cylinder in the flight attendant's car and trick her into driving to the neighbouring country, so the substitute pilot says that the young flyer has gone to a border town to identify a suspect.
She agrees to leave in the morning.
But then the radio reports the recovery of the young flyer's body.
Realizing her predicament, the flight attendant pretends not to have heard.
That night, finding some paint, she paints the aviator's three-star personal logo on the porch roof of the house.
Next day, back at the western city, the aviator learns the clerk has left the office—with the three men who knocked him out.
He and the manager then discover the clerk's eavesdropping device.
The aviator flies back to the crash area.
As his co-pilot he takes the mechanic, who works as the airline's mechanic because when he got his pilot's license he learned he was afraid to fly.
They see the three stars and land.
The aviator tells the mechanic that if there is any sign of trouble he must fly away and alert the air police.
When shots are fired, the mechanic does just that—not seeing the aviator and the flight attendant running for the plane.
The spies capture them both.
The substitute pilot and the spymaster depart in the substitute pilot's armed biplane, taking the flight attendant and the cylinder.
The mechanic then arrives with the air police, who capture the rest of the gang after a brief gunfight.
In a dogfight between biplanes, the spymaster is killed but the air police plane is shot down.
Now rescued, the aviator takes off with the mechanic.
He finds the substitute pilot's plane and executes risky maneuvers to force him to land.
The substitute pilot tries to run away and the mechanic throws a rock at him.
Both the flight attendant and the cylinder are recovered.
Although the government is grateful, all that the flight attendant and the aviator want to do is get married.
This is the story of the western city switchboard operator the young woman.
She learns from lawyer the attorney that she is actually the daughter of railroad tycoon the magnate.
She had been kidnapped as a baby by the magnate's brother and partner the uncle, and placed with strangers.
Once it is found out that she is an heiress, there is an attempt on her life by her bodyguard and chauffeur, which is foiled by the sleuth.
A telegram from her father is intercepted and replaced, telling her to meet him in the eastern city instead of the western city, and that a private train car has been arranged.
The young woman, the attorney, and her best friend the companion board the train bound for the eastern city.
In the private car, the lights go out and an announcement is heard, "Eight hours to live", after which the sleuth introduces himself to the young woman and her friends as a sleuth who prevents crime.
The sleuth reunites the young woman with her boyfriend the stowaway, who has stowed away.
Then the train is suddenly stopped until the wreck of a circus train on the tracks is cleared.
The attorney is murdered and "Five hours to live" is announced.
Then an escaped circus gorilla attacks the young woman, the companion, and the sleuth before jumping from the train to its death.
The next morning, the train stops in the same small town where the magnate's train has also stopped.
He has been tipped off by a mysterious voice transmission to meet her.

Now with no reason to go to the western city, her father joins the young woman's party in the private car, dismissing the danger, refusing to believe the other passenger when he says that the attorney was stabbed through the eye.

Suddenly, all the windows and doors are blocked with metal panels and the lights put out, and a voice informs the passengers that the private car is about to be uncoupled from the train and will roll backwards downhill towards another train, the express.
A secret panel opens, revealing concealed explosives that will make sure no one survives the crash.
The magnate recognizes the sinister voice as that of his brother, the uncle, who confirms his identity and says the magnate once cheated him.
The uncle uncouples the car and gasps.
The sleuth has shot him.
The dead body confirms his identity and reveals that he is the conductor in charge of the private car.
The magnate found the uncle's control center, and now he opens the shutters and uses a radio transmitter to broadcast a warning of the imminent collision and explosion.
The express's engineers reverse their train, but this also risks a collision since a freight train is following it.

A harrowing 10-minute segment ensues, cutting from the point of view of the passengers back and forth to the railway men frantically throwing switches and a series of harrowing near misses as they careen through a railway yard.
The express, the freight, and the runaway private car end on three separate tracks, but the private car is still plummeting downhill.
Then they dispatch a locomotive to catch up with the runaway car, warning its engineer about the explosives.
The near-misses continue as railway men risk their lives to keep the car on track.
The engine looms over the car.
The engineer manages to pull so close that—one by one—everyone can jump onto the small front platform of his steam locomotive.
He stops, just before the runaway car derails on a curve and explodes.
When everyone gets off to look, a blast of steam sends the sleuth and the companion into each other's arms.
When the steam finally clears, they dreamily exclaim “beautiful!” and skip off hand in hand.
The schoolteacher discovers the dead body of her colleague, music teacher the victim, in a schoolroom.
She summons her old friend, the inspector, but by the time he arrives, the corpse has disappeared.
Having watched the only entrance (other than a fire exit with an alarm), the schoolteacher knows the killer must still be inside.
When the police search the building, the detective is knocked out in the basement.
Meanwhile, the schoolteacher notices various clues, including a tune on the blackboard in the victim's classroom.
The body is found being burned in the basement furnace.
Then, the fire alarm goes off; the murderer has escaped.
The janitor, the school's drunkard janitor, had some financial quarrel with the victim.
The inspector arrests him, but the schoolteacher does not believe he is the one they are after.
She goes to the dead woman's apartment, which she had shared with her friend and school secretary, the secretary.
There, she discovers that the victim held one of the tickets for the lottery.
A newspaper account reports it is for the favorite in the race and is already worth $50,000.
If the horse were to win, the amount would be $300,000.
The secretary claims she had a half share in the ticket, giving her a motive for murder.
Fellow teacher the male teacher (the actor) admits that the victim was attracted to him.
The principal, the womanizing head of the school, asks the schoolteacher to investigate the crime, but suspiciously suggests she leave town to check out the victim's relatives.
Snooping around, she finds a fragment of a burnt love letter from him to the victim.
Later, during another search of the basement, the light is turned off and someone throws a hatchet at the schoolteacher's head.
After getting over her fright, she triumphantly points out to the inspector that the janitor could not be the killer, as he is still in jail.
Then, they see a newspaper report that he has escaped.
It is discovered that the victim was already dying of "pernicious anemia of the bones".
When the detective comes to in the hospital, he cannot remember what happened, but the schoolteacher has the inspector tell the newspapers that the detective knows the killer's identity.
When the murderer sneaks in to the detective's hospital room to poison his medicine, the trap is sprung.
The criminal turns out to be the male teacher.
(The tune on the blackboard spelled out the first few letters of his first name.)
Seeing no escape, the male teacher drinks the poison himself, but reveals his motive before dying.
The victim and he were secretly married last summer.
When his feelings changed, though, she would not give him up.
He tried poisoning her slowly (causing the anemia), but she became suspicious, forcing him to act more decisively.
Later, when the schoolteacher calls to console the secretary, she is disillusioned when the other detective answers the telephone and reveals he is having breakfast with the pretty woman.

Gentleman detective the sleuth begins an investigation when he receives an anonymous letter stating that society man the heir will be in danger when he appears at the casino owned by his uncle, the casino owner.
The sleuth visits the family estate, which is run by the mother, the matriarch of the household, and stumbles into one of the family's many quarrels.

At the end of the bitter quarrel, which involves the mother's son the heir and his wife the daughter-in-law, the daughter-in-law announces that she has decided to leave the house and go to another city.
During the tiff, the sleuth and the secretary (the mother's secretary) are introduced to each other and the secretary immediately takes a liking to the sleuth.
The sleuth takes the secretary to his home, where he and the district attorney show her the mysterious letter.
The secretary immediately recognizes the return address as being that of the family's townhouse in the small town, and notices that the letter was typed on her typewriter.
The sleuth assigns the sergeant to help stake out the casino that night, but their presence does not prevent the heir from suddenly collapsing at the card table.
At the same time, the secretary informs the sleuth that the daughter-in-law has died at the family house.

The district attorney begins his investigation of the murder by questioning the mother, who recalls having quarrelled with the daughter-in-law before she was poisoned, and the sister, the mother's daughter, who admits that she too had a spat with the daughter-in-law.

Meanwhile, the secretary finds the mother's recently altered will, in which she disinherited the casino owner, making it apparent that the heir and the sister would be the only ones who would benefit from the mother's death.
Other clues begin to surface, including the casino owner's unusual collection of books on chemistry and poisons, and a loaded gun found in the daughter-in-law's bedroom.
Soon after the heir's recovery, the mother is found dead of an apparent suicide, with a note, bearing her signature, in which she confesses to the daughter-in-law's murder.

Not convinced that the mystery has been solved, the sleuth pursues his theory, and discovers a secret laboratory where the casino owner has been making the newly discovered heavy water; it is not yet known whether this is a poison.
The casino owner holds the sleuth and the secretary captive at gunpoint, but they escape.
Still, the sleuth believes that the casino owner is not the murderer, but is merely one of many decoys set up by the real killer to lead the investigation astray.
The real killer turns out to be the heir, who gave himself a small dose of poison before.
He lures the sleuth and the secretary to the small-town townhouse to kill them.
But before the heir completes his "perfect crime", the sleuth reads from a letter he wrote earlier in which he detailed his theory about the killings.
In it, the sleuth names the heir as the murderer, calling him a rich, egomaniacal weakling, who, being tired of his wife, poisoned her and threw the blame on his uncle, whom he despised.
After hearing the sleuth's summary of the murder plot, the heir tells his captors that he has arranged to pin the sleuth and the secretary's forthcoming murder on the casino owner.
However, when the heir shoots the sleuth, the sergeant and others emerge from behind a door where they have been recording the heir's confession and shoot him dead.
After thanking the mother's maid the servant for loading the heir's gun with blanks, the sleuth resumes his romance with the secretary.
The detective is brought in when an archaeologist disappears while excavating ancient art treasures in the desert country.

The detective must sort out the stories of the archaeological team, deal with the crazed son of the missing scientist, learn why priceless treasures are falling into the hands of private collectors, and battle many seemingly supernatural events.
The detective's initial journey begins with a rickety biplane ride and then a desert trip by pack mule ("Offspring of the devil", mutters the detective at his animal).
But there are more creature comforts at the professor's mansion, where the detective meets his beautiful daughter the young woman.
The Professor has been missing two weeks, and the young woman vehemently defends him against charges of dishonesty.
And her boyfriend the young man vehemently defends the daughter.

The doctor has loaned the expedition a large amount of money when it began to run out of funds; and the other professor confesses that the items that turned up in museums had been sold by him, also to replenish funding.
The young woman's brother the violinist has been rendered lame by an accident at the site, and is prone to playing sad songs on his violin.
Servant girl the maid is in the background, innocent, but acting a little suspiciously, perhaps to confuse the questions of who done it, or who is in on it.
Butler the manservant says the family is "marked for death" for violating the tomb.
The other family servant, the helper, can be described as "weak but willing" when it comes to danger.
There is a complete scientific laboratory in the basement, to catalogue discoveries.
The detective notices the seal on a sarcophagus has been broken.
They X-ray it and discover a 20th-century bullet lodged in the "Mummy", which turns out to be the professor's corpse; drained of blood and mummified to remove giveaway decay.
The young woman has suffered unexplained attacks of sleepiness and anxiety; the detective discovers her personal cigarettes had been laced with a hallucinatory drug.
While playing his violin, the violinist suddenly keels over dead.
Butler the manservant flees rather than be questioned, which throws suspicion on him.
Local policeman the inspector is overly formal but competent; and requests the detective's assistance.
The detective discounts the supernatural, as the murders have been committed by someone with sharp knowledge of modern science.
He discovers that the violinist had been killed when a high note from his violin shattered a glass vial filled with poison gas.
Exploring the tomb at night with an eager young man, they discover a secret room that can be reached only while swimming underwater.
The contents are many looted treasures and some elaborate "ghost" disguises.
It also contains the murderer, who shoots the young man point blank.
The detective and the helper manage to get the young man back to the mansion, where he hovers between life and death.
The detective says since he was shot from the front, he must know the killer's identity and will reveal it when he recovers.
This is the cue for the murderer to try to finish the job; but the detective and a small brigade of Egyptian police are waiting and take the killer into custody.
Spotting the young woman and the young man embracing, the detective declares this is all the reward he requires for his efforts.

The detective is on his way back from completing the other-city case—they always mentioned the previous case—to go on "vacation" to the city, but this is just a way to make people think that he is innocently there.
He is on a case for some other-city bankers and customers who say that some bonds from the bank in the city are forged, so they hired the detective to solve the case.
The detective is on his way to meet the new ward of the head of the bank, the banker.
A blind man named the beggar comes up to him, and asks him for some change.
After a police officer escorts the beggar away, the detective calls his assistant, the agent, who promises to talk with him later about new information she found out.
He meets with the young man, the banker's ward who is about to own the bank.
The detective also meets the young man's friends: the artist, an alcoholic painter and his girlfriend, and the fiancée, the daughter of the banker.
The young man tells the detective that the fiancée is the special one: the two are engaged.
That night, the detective, the artist and his girlfriend, the fiancée, and the young man go to a cafe/club, where the agent works as a dancer.
After her performance, she is thrown into a room by her dance partner (part of the routine), where the beggar murders her by throwing a knife at her.
Her last words to the detective instruct him to look in her apartment, where he finds a letter hidden in a cuckoo clock which explains that the former suitor is spending beyond his income.
As the detective leaves the agent's house, the beggar throws a giant rock down in an attempt to kill him, which fails.
He goes home and reveals his secret to the eldest son, his #1 son.
That night, another attempt is made on the detective's life, this time with another thrown knife.
However, the detective has outsmarted the culprit by throwing pillows onto his bed.
The next morning, he interviews the banker.
As he is leaving, he sees the beggar making a scene, as he feels that the bank is cheating him out of his money.
His escort gets him to leave, but not before he threatens everyone there.
The detective instructs the eldest son to do some spy work around town.
The detective is then accosted by his old friend, an inspector.
They go and eat together.
Later, the young man drops the fiancée off at her house.
However, after the young man leaves, she goes to the former suitor's apartment to get some love letters, which she doesn't want the young man to see.
The former suitor is seen calling a mysterious person, revealing that he is in the forging business.
Unbeknownst to him, the beggar is secretly watching him through the window.
The former suitor welcomes the fiancée in.
As he is about to give her the letters, he is shot by an unseen assailant.
The other tenants rush up after the fiancée screams.
They believe her to be the murderer.
She is jailed by the inspector, but the detective points out an overlooked clue: footprints leading to the former suitor's room.
They release the fiancée.
That night, the detective goes to the bank and asks the bank manager, the official, to give him the beggar's address.
Afterwards, they catch the artist in the act of leaving town.
The eldest son keeps the artist company while the detective goes with the young man to the beggar's house.
They are followed by the beggar as they make their way to the basement.
Inside, they discover printing machines.
The beggar comes in and shoots at the detective, but the detective is revealed to have blocked it.
They capture the beggar as the eldest son and the police arrive.
The detective reveals that the beggar is the murderer, but he is not a real person.
He has "the beggar" take off his false face.
